Real-Time Acoustic Anomaly Detection in Vehicles Using AI Processor and      
Machine Learning 
Attila Aradi1,2 
, Attila Károly Varga2 
  
 
1.ION-Technik Kft., Tarnaszentmária, Hungary 
2.Institute of Automation and Infocommunication, University of Miskolc, Miskolc, Hungary 
 
Abstract 
This study investigates real-time acoustic anomaly detection in vehicles, focusing on diesel 
particulate filter (DPF) faults in a pickup truck as a case study. Utilizing two WAV audio recordings—
one from normal idling and another during a DPF fault—features such as Mel-Frequency Cepstral 
Coefficients (MFCC) and Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) were extracted. Machine learning 
models, including Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), were 
deployed on the Hailo-8 AI processor for edge-based, real-time inference. The approach achieved high 
accuracy in anomaly classification, demonstrating the viability of embedded AI for predictive vehicle 
maintenance. This non-invasive method enhances fault detection speed and efficiency, reducing 
downtime and emissions in automotive applications. The edge computing approach demonstrates 
significant advantages over cloud-based alternatives: sub-millisecond inference latency enables 
immediate fault detection critical for preventing vehicle damage; continuous operation without network 
dependency ensures reliability in areas with poor connectivity; local processing eliminates security risks 
associated with transmitting sensitive vehicle data; and bandwidth requirements are reduced as only 
anomaly alerts require transmission. Hailo-8's power-efficient architecture enables continuous 
monitoring without significant battery drain, while its 26 TOPS performance capability ensures real-
time processing of complex acoustic signatures. This non-invasive method enhances fault detection 
speed and efficiency, reducing downtime and emissions in automotive applications while providing a 
scalable solution deployable across entire vehicle fleets without cloud infrastructure dependencies.  
 
Keywords: Acoustic anomaly detection; Machine Learning; edge-computing; cloud computing; AI processor

1. Introduction  
Modern vehicles increasingly rely on advanced diagnostic 
systems to maintain performance and comply with emission 
standards. Anomalies, such as faults in diesel particulate filters 
(DPF), can lead to inefficiencies, increased emissions, and me-
chanical failures if not detected promptly [3]. Traditional meth-
ods, including onboard diagnostics (OBD), often require inva-
sive procedures or post-event analysis, limiting their real-time 
applicability. Acoustic anomaly detection emerges as a non-in-
vasive alternative, leveraging engine sounds captured via micro-
phones to identify deviations in real-time using artificial intelli-
gence (AI) and machine learning (ML) [2]. 
This research targets vehicles like the truck, where DPF faults 
manifest as subtle acoustic changes due to altered exhaust dy-
namics [5]. By integrating edge AI processors such as Hailo-8 
(part number HNC18BC21BH), we enable low-latency, on-de-
vice processing suitable for embedded systems. Prior studies 
have shown the efficacy of ML in acoustic fault detection, but 
real-time deployment in vehicles remains underexplored [1]. 
This work advances the field by combining acoustic signal pro-
cessing with specialized AI hardware for scalable, real-time 
anomaly detection. 
 
2. Research Methods 
2.1. Data Collection 
Audio data was collected from a Diesel engine compartment us-
ing an acoustic microphone. Small sound clips of WAV files at 
44.1 kHz sampling rate were recorded: one during normal idle op-
eration and another post-DPF fault indication via the malfunction 
lamp.

2.2. Feature Extraction 
Signals were preprocessed with bandpass filtering (100-5000 
Hz) to isolate engine-relevant frequencies. Features included: 
MFCC: 13 coefficients extracted via Librosa to capture perceptual 
audio traits [1]. DWT: Daubechies wavelet (db4) for time-fre-
quency decomposition, emphasizing transient anomalies [4]. 
Spectrograms: Generated via STFT for CNN input. These features 
highlight acoustic deviations caused by faults like DPF clogging 
[7].

M.2 module into the vehicle’s computing setup. 
3. Results and Discussion 
The SVM model attained 92% accuracy, with MFCC features 
effectively detecting low-frequency shifts from DPF faults. The 
CNN, accelerated by Hailo-8 (HNC18BC21BH), reached 96% ac-
curacy and processed data in real-time (< 50 ms latency), outper-
forming non-edge methods. Confusion matrices showed low false 
negatives, crucial for safety. 
Results align with studies on acoustic ML for vehicles, where 
anomalies like irregular harmonics indicate faults [8]. Hailo-8’s 
(HNC18BC21BH) edge processing reduces latency compared to 
cloud alternatives, enabling applications in autonomous and fleet 
vehicles. Limitations include noise sensitivity; future multi- sensor 
fusion could enhance robustness [9]. This method could cut 
maintenance costs by 20-30% through early detection [16].  
3.1 Edge Processing vs. Cloud Alternatives: A Detailed Analysis 
of Latency Reduction in the Context of truck Acoustic Anomaly 
Detection 
In the specific case of acoustic anomaly detection for diesel partic-
ulate filter (DPF) faults in the Diesel pickup truck, edge processing—
enabled by embedded AI hardware like the Hailo-8 processor (part 
number HNC18BC21BH)—offers significant latency advantages 
over cloud-based alternatives. This analysis focuses on how edge 
computing minimizes delays in processing acoustic signals from en-
gine recordings, ensuring real-time fault detection that is critical for 
vehicle safety, maintenance, and emission control [11]. We will ex-
amine the mechanisms, quantitative comparisons, implications for 
the truck application, trade-offs, and future outlook, tailored to this 
automotive diagnostic scenario. 
3.1.1. Understanding Latency in truck Acoustic Anomaly Detec-
tion 
In the pick-up truck setup, latency refers to the time from capturing 
an acoustic signal (e.g., a 30-second WAV file at 44.1 kHz from the 
engine compartment) to generating an anomaly alert (e.g., DPF fault 
detection via machine learning models like SVM or CNN). Key con-
tributors to latency include data transmission, feature extraction (e.g., 
MFCC or DWT), model inference, and response delivery. Cloud-
Based Approach: Audio data is uploaded to remote servers for pro-
cessing. For a diesel vehicle in a remote or mobile environment (e.g., 
off-road or fleet operations), this involves transmitting raw or prepro-
cessed data over cellular networks (4G/5G) or Wi-Fi to cloud plat-
forms like AWS or Azure. Delays arise from network RTT (50-200 
ms for urban areas, up to 500 ms in rural zones), data compres-
sion/upload time (seconds for large files), server queuing during peak 
loads, and inference on shared resources [23]. Edge Processing Ap-
proach: Using Hailo-8 embedded in the vehicle’s onboard system 
(e.g., as an M.2 module integrated with an external on board diagnos-
tic unit), data is processed locally. This eliminates long-distance 
transfers, confining operations to on-device hardware, resulting in la-
tencies under 50 ms for end-to-end detection. The primary mecha-
nism for reduction is local computation proximity: In cloud setups, 
even optimized audio streams (e.g., compressed to 1-5 MB) face in-
herent network bottlenecks, while edge leverages the Hailo- 8’s 26 
TOPS performance to handle spectrogram-based CNN inference di-
rectly on microphone-captured data. 
3.1.2. Quantitative Comparison of Latency for truck Application 
Based on benchmarks from similar acoustic AI systems and Hailo-
8 specifications, edge processing reduces latency by 70-95% in vehi-
cle diagnostics [15]. Consider a typical DPF fault detection cycle: 
capturing idle engine sound, extracting features, classifying anoma-
lies, and alerting the driver. As shown in Table 1, edge computing 
using the Hailo-8 processor significantly reduces latency compared 
to cloud-based processing across all aspects of data handling in a 
truck scenario, system architecture shown Figure 1. The critical im-
portance of millisecond-level detection speed in vehicle anomaly de-
tection cannot be overstated. In diesel vehicles with DPF systems, 
rapid detection enables immediate corrective actions before fault es-
calation. For instance, a DPF reaching critical pressure levels can 
cause engine stalling or permanent damage within seconds. With mil-
lisecond response times, the system can trigger emergency regenera-
tion cycles or alert drivers to immediately reduce engine load, pre-
venting catastrophic failures. Furthermore, rapid anomaly detection 
is essential for emissions compliance delayed detection of DPF mal-
functions can result in excessive particulate emissions exceeding reg-
ulatory limits within minutes. The sub-millisecond processing capa-
bility of edge computing also enables real-time correlation of acoustic 
patterns with other sensor data (temperature, pressure, vibration), 
providing a comprehensive fault diagnosis that cloud-based systems 
with multi-second latencies simply cannot achieve in safety-critical 
scenarios. For instance, data transmission latency decreases from 
100–400 ms in cloud environments to 10 ms on the edge, achieving

3.1.3. Mechanisms Driving Latency Reduction in truck Context 
Tailored to the truck acoustic system, edge processing leverages: 
Minimized Network Overhead: Cloud requires sending data to serv-
ers, introducing variable delays from truck’s mobile use (e.g., varying 
signal strength in pickup trucks). Edge confines data to the vehicle’s 
internal network, using PCIe interfaces for near-zero transmission 
time. Hardware Optimization for Audio Tasks: Hailo-8’s dataflow 
architecture excels in low-power inference (2.5W), processing spec-
trograms from engine microphones without offloading. This con-
trasts with cloud GPUs, which may throttle for cost-efficiency, add-
ing 100-300 ms [18]. Data Reduction at Source: In edge mode, raw 
WAV files are filtered locally (e.g., bandpass 100- 5000 Hz), sending 
only anomaly summaries to the cloud if needed—reducing upload 
latency by 80-90% for telematics in truck fleets. Real-Time Stream-
ing Protocols: Edge supports low-overhead protocols like those in au-
tomotive CAN buses, enabling continuous monitoring without the 
HTTP overhead of cloud APIs. Cloud alternatives, while scalable for 
aggregating fleet data (e.g., training models on multiple truck vehi-
cles), are hindered by physical distances and bandwidth limits, mak-
ing them unsuitable for real-time DPF monitoring where delays could 
lead to emission non-compliance or breakdowns [20]. 
3.1.4  Implications for truck Anomaly Detection 
In practice, edge processing transforms truck diagnostics: Safety 
and Reliability: Real-time detection (<100 ms) allows immediate

alerts for DPF faults, pre-venting overpressure issues that could cause 
engine stall vital for truck’s rugged, off-road applications [19]. Cost 
and Efficiency Savings: Reduced latency minimizes downtime; a 20-
30% maintenance cost cut is possible, as per automotive AI studies, 
by enabling predictive fixes before faults escalate [21]. Emission 
Control: Faster anomaly spotting ensures timely DPF regeneration, 
aiding compliance with standards like Euro 6 in truck models. Inte-
gration with Vehicle Systems: Hailo-8 embeds seamlessly with 
OBD-II, providing hybrid edge-cloud setups where edge handles ur-
gent tasks and cloud analyzes trends. However, cloud excels in post-
processing large datasets from multiple diesel vehicles for model re-
training, complementing edge for long-term insights [22]. 
3.1.5  Potential Drawbacks and Trade-Offs in truck Scenario 
Hardware Limitations: Hailo-8’s compact design suits truck’s en-
gine bay but has finite memory (no external DRAM needed), poten-
tially slowing complex multi-fault models compared to cloud’s scala-
bility. Environmental Challenges: In harsh truck conditions (dust, vi-
bration), edge hardware must be ruggedized, increasing upfront costs 
(∼$100-200 per unit) versus cloud’s pay-per-use model. Security: 
Edge reduces data exposure but requires robust on-device encryption 
for acoustic logs, unlike centralized cloud security [12]. Hybrid Mit-
igation: For truck fleets, edge processes real-time anomalies locally, 
syncing summaries to the cloud—balancing latency with analytics 
[13]. 
3.1.6  Future Trends and Conclusions for truck Applications 
With advancements in 5G-V2X (Vehicle-to-Everything), edge la-
tency could drop to <10 ms in connected truck vehicles by 2025-2030, 
enhancing ADAS integration. Emerging chips like next-gen Hailo 
could support multimodal fusion (audio + vibration), further reducing 
delays [14]. 
In summary, for truck acoustic anomaly detection, edge processing 
drastically cuts latency versus cloud alternatives by localizing com-
putation, ensuring real-time responsiveness essential for safety and 
efficiency. This non-invasive, embedded approach not only outper-
forms traditional diagnostics but also paves the way for smarter, more 
reliable vehicles, with hybrid models offering the best of both worlds 
[10].
